item.title: The Potty-Training Plot Twist Nobody Wants
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Vaginitis is inflammation of the vagina or vestibule in female dogs — spayed or intact — and one of its sneakiest features is that it can look almost exactly like potty-training regression
  • It is split into two main types: juvenile vaginitis, which affects female puppies before their first heat and often resolves on its own once they mature, and adult vaginitis, which tends to have a clearer underlying cause and usually shows more pronounced symptoms
  • Causes range widely, including bacterial or viral infections, urinary tract infections, urine pooling, foreign bodies, hormonal imbalances, vaginal trauma, and anatomical issues
  • Diagnosing vaginitis can be tricky because symptoms overlap with UTIs and free-catch urine samples can be contaminated by vaginal bacteria
  • Most cases respond well to treatment within a few weeks, and puppies often outgrow it after their first heat cycle — though dogs with a recessed vulva may eventually require surgery to keep flare-ups from coming back

Your puppy was doing so well. She had figured out the back door, she was holding it overnight, and you were starting to feel like you had cracked the code. Then, almost overnight, the accidents started again. She squats every few minutes. She licks at herself constantly. There might be a tiny smear of discharge on the floor. You assume she is regressing — or that you are failing — and you brace for another month of crate schedules and treat pouches.

Except this might not be a training problem at all. There is a real medical condition that can pose almost exactly as backslidden potty training in young female dogs, and it has a name: vaginitis.

What Vaginitis Actually Is

Vaginitis is the medical term for inflammation of the vagina or the vestibule (the area just inside the vulva). It can show up in any female dog — spayed or intact, puppy or adult — but it is especially common in young female puppies who have not yet gone through their first heat.1,2

It is not, despite the name, the same thing as a urinary tract infection (UTI). A UTI is an infection of the bladder and urethra (and may include the kidneys and ureters). Vaginitis is inflammation of the vagina or vestibule itself. The two can produce overlapping symptoms — which is part of what makes the condition so easy to misread.3

Why It Gets Mistaken for a Training Issue

The classic vaginitis picture looks a lot like a puppy who suddenly forgot her house manners. She urinates more often, sometimes in small amounts. She has accidents indoors. She licks herself frequently. There may be a sticky, clear-to-cloudy discharge that you only notice when she has been sitting on the rug.

If you have been deep in training mode, your first instinct is usually to add more potty breaks, tighten the schedule, or try a different routine. None of that fixes the underlying problem, because the underlying problem is not behavior. It is inflammation.

The other reason it gets missed: many vaginitis pups do not act sick at all. They eat, play, and feel fine. There is no fever, no big drama — just the constant licking and the suspiciously frequent squats.4,5

2 Main Types of Vaginitis

Veterinarians generally split vaginitis into two categories based on when it shows up. The timing is not just a label — it usually points to different likely causes, different treatment paths, and a different prognosis. Knowing which version your dog is dealing with helps shape what to expect and how aggressively to investigate the underlying cause:6

  • Juvenile (or prepubertal) vaginitis affects female puppies under a year of age, before they have gone through their first heat cycle. It is often discovered almost by accident during a routine exam, or because a pet parent notices the constant licking and discharge.
  • Adult vaginitis shows up later in life and is more often seen in spayed females. It usually is chronic and is secondary to a clearer underlying cause — anatomical, infectious, or related to urine or fecal contamination of the area. In rare cases, it can be secondary to a vaginal or vulvar tumor. Symptoms can look similar to the puppy version but tend to be more pronounced.

What Causes It

Vaginitis is more of a final common pathway that several different problems can lead to — there is not just one trigger. Possible causes include:7

  • A prepubertal, sexually immature vagina or vulva that has not yet fully developed
  • Urinary tract infections that contaminate or irritate the vaginal area
  • Urinary incontinence or urine pooling around the vulva
  • Bacterial or viral infections
  • Anatomical abnormalities, including a recessed or hooded vulva
  • Foreign bodies — grass awns, plant material, or other debris
  • Vaginal trauma, including from mating
  • Vaginal hematomas, abscesses, or tumors
  • Ectopic ureters (where the ureter empties in the wrong place)
  • Hormonal imbalances or chemical irritation

Identifying the root cause is the key to treating vaginitis effectively, because without it, the same inflammation tends to come right back.

Recessed Vulvas and Breeds at Risk

One of the more common anatomical setups behind chronic vaginitis is a recessed or hooded vulva. This is exactly what it sounds like — the vulva is partially tucked under a fold of skin instead of being out in the open. The fold traps moisture, urine, and bacteria, creating an environment that vaginitis loves.

Breeds with extra skin folds and flatter conformations are more prone to recessed vulvas. French Bulldogs, English Bulldogs, and Pugs come up frequently, but the issue is also seen in Labrador Retrievers, Golden Retrievers, and many other breeds. Excess body weight can make a borderline case worse, since extra weight can deepen the skin folds.8,9

Vaginitis Signs to Watch For

If your dog is dealing with vaginitis, the signs may come and go and can range from subtle to obvious. Common ones include:10,11,12

  • Frequent urination, often in small amounts
  • Indoor accidents, especially in a previously house-trained dog
  • Excessive licking of the vulvar area
  • Scooting or rubbing the rear end on the floor
  • Visible discharge — clear, cloudy, yellow, pus-like, or, less commonly, bloody
  • Redness or swelling around the vulva
  • A noticeable odor
  • Discomfort while urinating
  • Male dogs paying unusual attention to her (vaginitis can attract males even in spayed females)

Most vaginitis puppies feel just fine otherwise. If your dog is lethargic, off her food, vomiting, running a fever, or seems painful, that is a sign something bigger is going on and needs prompt veterinary attention.

Why Diagnosing It Can Be Tricky

Here is where things get a little complicated. The symptoms of vaginitis and a UTI can look almost identical from the outside — both can cause frequent urination, licking, and discomfort. Even on a urinalysis, the line between the two can blur.

That is because the way a urine sample is collected matters. A free-catch sample (where urine is caught in a clean container while the dog pees) can pick up bacteria from the vagina, the dog's environment, or the container itself. So if that sample comes back positive for bacteria, it is not always clear where the bacteria are actually coming from.

Cystocentesis — collecting a urine sample directly from the bladder using a needle guided by ultrasound — gives a sterile sample. If bacteria show up there, you know they are in the bladder. If the bladder sample is clean but symptoms persist, the infection is likely further downstream, in the vagina or vestibule.13

How Veterinarians Sort It Out

Diagnosis usually starts with a thorough physical exam and a careful look at the vulvar area for redness, swelling, discharge, or anatomical issues like a recessed vulva. Beyond that, your vet may use:14,15

  • Urinalysis to check for bladder involvement
  • Microscopic examination of any discharge
  • Culture and sensitivity testing of vaginal or urine samples to identify specific bacteria and guide antibiotic choice
  • Vaginal cytology to look at the cells in the area
  • Vaginoscopy, which involves using a small camera to look inside the vagina for foreign bodies or growths
  • Ultrasound or contrast radiographs (X-rays) to rule out anatomical abnormalities
  • Blood work to screen for underlying conditions

The reason for the layered workup is simple. Vaginitis is often a clue rather than a stand-alone diagnosis. Finding the contributing factor, be it a UTI, a foreign body, or an anatomical issue — is what makes treatment actually stick.

The Treatment Depends on the Cause

Mild juvenile vaginitis with minimal symptoms often needs little more than keeping the area clean and waiting. Many cases resolve on their own as the puppy matures and goes through her first heat cycle. When treatment is needed, it usually targets whatever is driving the inflammation. Possibilities include:16,17,18

  • Antibiotics — If a bacterial cause is identified, your veterinarian will choose an antibiotic based on culture and sensitivity testing. When empirical treatment is needed before culture results, amoxicillin-clavulanate is often effective against the bacteria most commonly involved.
  • Vaginal or vulvar douches — Mild antiseptic rinses (usually dilute chlorhexidine or povidone-iodine) may be used under veterinary direction to help reduce bacterial load and inflammation. These should never be done at home without specific instructions.
  • Treating any underlying problem — If a UTI is involved, that gets its own targeted treatment. If urinary incontinence is contributing, that needs its own workup. Foreign bodies are removed, hematomas or abscesses are addressed, and tumors are evaluated separately.
  • Hygiene support — For dogs with skin folds or a hooded vulva, daily cleaning of the area with vet-approved wipes (often containing chlorhexidine) can help reduce flare-ups. Keeping bedding clean and dry helps too.

When Surgery Comes Into the Picture

If a recessed vulva is causing recurring vaginitis that does not respond to medical treatment, surgery may be the most lasting fix. A procedure called vulvoplasty removes the excess skin around the vulva so that urine can drain freely and moisture does not get trapped in folds.

This surgery is usually reserved for serious or complicated cases — especially when urine pooling is clearly contributing to the problem. Veterinarians typically recommend waiting until the dog is fully grown before performing it, and an Elizabethan collar (cone) during recovery is essential to prevent licking.19,20

The Good News

Most cases of vaginitis respond well to conservative care. Many dogs are back to normal within two or three weeks of starting treatment. For puppies, the picture is even more reassuring — most cases resolve on their own once they go through their first heat cycle and the vagina matures.

In chronic cases or those tied to anatomical issues, the picture is more dog-specific. The prognosis usually depends on how severe and how long-standing the problem is, and whether the underlying cause can be identified and addressed. With the right plan, even recurring cases can be brought under control.21

What This Means if You Are in the Middle of It

If your previously house-trained puppy suddenly seems to be unraveling, take a breath before you start rewriting the training plan. Look for the extra signs: the licking, the small puddles, any discharge, any redness, the squatting without much coming out. These are not behavior signals. They are medical ones.

A call to your veterinarian is the right first step. A focused exam, possibly a urine sample, and sometimes a quick look at the vulvar area can answer the question fast. Bring along a description of how often she is urinating, what the discharge looks like (a quick phone photo is fine), and how long the symptoms have been going on.

If your dog is older and has a recessed vulva or recurring issues, the same advice applies — keep notes, watch for patterns, and do not wait it out. The earlier the underlying cause is found, the easier vaginitis usually is to manage.

Trust What Your Pet’s Body Is Telling You

Potty training is hard enough without an invisible medical complication thrown into the mix. Vaginitis is the kind of condition that quietly hides behind "she's regressing" or "she just won't get it" — when actually, your dog is not being stubborn. She is uncomfortable, and her body is trying to tell you so.

The good news is that vaginitis is almost always treatable, and very often self-resolves with time and a good veterinary partner. So if your house-training plot has taken an unexpected turn, take it seriously, but do not panic. A check-in with your veterinarian usually clears up the mystery — and gets your puppy back on track, in more ways than one.

  • 2,5,6,10,15,16,20 Merck Manual, September 2024
  • 3,4,8,11,13,17,19 American Kennel Club, April 4, 2025
  • 9 J Am Vet Med Assoc. 2021 Oct 1;259(7):744-748

item.title: From Super Aggressive to 'Highly Adoptable' in Only 10 Days
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Researchers in Australia studied the effects of “gentling” on shelter cats
  • Gentling involves a way of interacting with sheltered cats to reduce their stress level, maintain their health, and improve their level of contentment
  • Even aggressive, hostile cats destined for euthanasia respond well to gentling, making them much more likely to be adopted
  • Emotional stress in shelter cats suppresses the immune system, leading to upper respiratory infections — the second leading cause of euthanasia in shelters
  • Content cats show higher blood levels of S-IgA, an infection-fighting antibody highly responsive to emotional states

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published December 21, 2015.

Well here’s some purr-fectly cheery news! Researchers at the University of Queensland in Australia have scientifically proven that petting, brushing, and playing with shelter cats — a practice known as “gentling” — helps keep them healthy. And healthy, content cats are much more likely to find new forever homes.

Health, Well-Being of Shelter Cats Improves with Gentling

The University of Queensland study, published in the journal Preventive Veterinary Medicine,1 looked at 96 shelter cats judged to be healthy and content.

The cats were divided into two groups. Group 1 cats were given positive attention from the same person for 10-minute sessions, four times a day, for 10 days. During the gentling sessions, the kitties received petting, brushing, and playtime with their designated person.

Group 2 cats (the control group), got nothing more than a person standing in front of their cage, eyes averted, on the same schedule (10 minutes at a time, four times a day, for 10 days).

At the end of the 10 days, the kitties in group 1 remained content, and fewer had upper respiratory infections. (Respiratory disorders are a response to stress commonly seen in shelter cats.)

Sadly, the group 2 cats were less content at the end of the study, and more were sick. Of the 49 cats in the control group, 17 developed respiratory disorders, compared with only 9 of the 47 cats in the gentling group.

Study co-author Nadine Gourkow, an animal welfare consultant, told The Huffington Post she found a “strong association between positive emotions induced by gentling and good health” in the cats.2 This is probably due to the fact that happy cats produce more antibodies, and more antibodies mean a greater ability to fight off illness.

“We have learned that the domestic cat is very responsive to good treatment by humans,” says Gourkow’s colleague and co-author Clive J.C. Phillips of the University of Queensland.3

Content Cats Have Higher Levels of Infection-Fighting Antibodies

The gentling study was funded by the Morris Animal Foundation with the goal of helping shelter cats stay healthy, and therefore, more adoptable.

Emotional stress in cats results in compromised immune function, which commonly leads to upper respiratory infections (URIs). URIs are the second leading cause of euthanasia in shelter cats because the infections are expensive to treat and highly contagious.

According to study co-author Phillips, the researchers, “Examined the relationships among behavior, the stress hormone cortisol, and levels of secretory immunoglobulin A (S-IgA) in shelter cats.

S-IgA is a substance that helps the immune system launch a response against URIs and it is highly responsive to emotional states. In other species, emotional stress was shown to inhibit S-IgA, and increasing emotional well-being stimulates S-IgA.”4

The researchers looked at three different emotional states in the cats — anxiety, frustration, and contentment, and observed that content kitties had higher blood levels of S-IgA.

The group 1 cats were given gentling to reduce anxiety, training to decrease frustration, and positive interactions with humans to help maintain contentment. The researchers discovered that all 3 types of interventions increased and helped maintain the cats’ contentment, and stimulated S-IgA.

And in fact, several kitties who had displayed high levels of aggression and hostility when they entered the shelter responded to the interventions within just six days, and quickly found new homes.

Aggressive Jack the Shelter Cat Gets Gentled and Adopted

Jack the cat, a stray, was picked up by a humane officer, and brought to a shelter. The shelter staff suspected the cat had serious dental problems, but he wouldn’t allow handling. In fact, poor Jack was very frightened and aggressive towards anyone who came near his cage.

The protocol in many shelters is to euthanize stray cats after a legal holding period of 72 hours if they are deemed unadoptable due to a medical condition or behavioral issues such as severe aggression.

Jack was enrolled in the University of Queensland study. However, his behavior was such that he couldn’t be provided with gentling interventions by hand. Instead, his handler attempted interaction using a stick and rubber ball.

During the first attempt, Jack was very aggressive with the handler, hissing and attacking the stick with the ball attached. However, after a few sessions, the cat started to relax, and allowed himself to be handled. Jack’s stress level remained high, but he was no longer hissing or growling, and by day 4, he was purring and rubbing up against his person’s hand.

By day 10, Jack was deemed “highly adoptable.” He was neutered, received much-needed dental care, and was adopted soon after.

The researchers believe gentling improved Jack’s welfare at the shelter and saved his life. According to Morris Animal Foundation, “He and thousands like him are usually considered non-adoptable and euthanized within a few days of entering the shelter.”5

Gentling Could Help Other Shelter Animals As Well

The researchers will use their study results to create educational materials for use by shelter personnel and veterinary staffs to improve the emotional well-being and health of cats.

Gourkow and Phillips plan to continue their research into gentling by looking next at which methods are most effective. Also on Gourkow’s to-do list is a website to teach shelters how to apply gentling techniques, along with other methods for keeping kitty residents healthy, happy, and optimally adoptable.

The researchers believe gentling might provide similar benefits to other shelter animals as well, for example, dogs with kennel cough. For a good gentling primer, read Handling & Gentling by the Peninsula Humane Society & SPCA.

  • 1 Preventive Veterinary Medicine, Vol 121, Iss 3-4, 1 October 2015, pp 288-296
  • 2,3 Huffington Post, October 6, 2015
  • 4,5 Morris Animal Foundation (Archived)

Well here’s some purr-fectly cheery news! Researchers at the University of Queensland in Australia have scientifically proven that petting, brushing, and playing with shelter cats — a practice known as “gentling” — helps keep them healthy. And healthy, content cats are much more likely to find new forever homes.

Health, Well-Being of Shelter Cats Improves with Gentling

The University of Queensland study, published in the journal Preventive Veterinary Medicine,1 looked at 96 shelter cats judged to be healthy and content.

The cats were divided into two groups. Group 1 cats were given positive attention from the same person for 10-minute sessions, four times a day, for 10 days. During the gentling sessions, the kitties received petting, brushing, and playtime with their designated person.

Group 2 cats (the control group), got nothing more than a person standing in front of their cage, eyes averted, on the same schedule (10 minutes at a time, four times a day, for 10 days).

At the end of the 10 days, the kitties in group 1 remained content, and fewer had upper respiratory infections. (Respiratory disorders are a response to stress commonly seen in shelter cats.)

Sadly, the group 2 cats were less content at the end of the study, and more were sick. Of the 49 cats in the control group, 17 developed respiratory disorders, compared with only 9 of the 47 cats in the gentling group.

Study co-author Nadine Gourkow, an animal welfare consultant, told The Huffington Post she found a “strong association between positive emotions induced by gentling and good health” in the cats.2 This is probably due to the fact that happy cats produce more antibodies, and more antibodies mean a greater ability to fight off illness.

“We have learned that the domestic cat is very responsive to good treatment by humans,” says Gourkow’s colleague and co-author Clive J.C. Phillips of the University of Queensland.3

Content Cats Have Higher Levels of Infection-Fighting Antibodies

The gentling study was funded by the Morris Animal Foundation with the goal of helping shelter cats stay healthy, and therefore, more adoptable.

Emotional stress in cats results in compromised immune function, which commonly leads to upper respiratory infections (URIs). URIs are the second leading cause of euthanasia in shelter cats because the infections are expensive to treat and highly contagious.

According to study co-author Phillips, the researchers, “Examined the relationships among behavior, the stress hormone cortisol, and levels of secretory immunoglobulin A (S-IgA) in shelter cats.

S-IgA is a substance that helps the immune system launch a response against URIs and it is highly responsive to emotional states. In other species, emotional stress was shown to inhibit S-IgA, and increasing emotional well-being stimulates S-IgA.”4

The researchers looked at three different emotional states in the cats — anxiety, frustration, and contentment, and observed that content kitties had higher blood levels of S-IgA.

The group 1 cats were given gentling to reduce anxiety, training to decrease frustration, and positive interactions with humans to help maintain contentment. The researchers discovered that all 3 types of interventions increased and helped maintain the cats’ contentment, and stimulated S-IgA.

And in fact, several kitties who had displayed high levels of aggression and hostility when they entered the shelter responded to the interventions within just six days, and quickly found new homes.

Jack the cat, a stray, was picked up by a humane officer, and brought to a shelter. The shelter staff suspected the cat had serious dental problems, but he wouldn’t allow handling. In fact, poor Jack was very frightened and aggressive towards anyone who came near his cage.

The protocol in many shelters is to euthanize stray cats after a legal holding period of 72 hours if they are deemed unadoptable due to a medical condition or behavioral issues such as severe aggression.

Jack was enrolled in the University of Queensland study. However, his behavior was such that he couldn’t be provided with gentling interventions by hand. Instead, his handler attempted interaction using a stick and rubber ball.

The researchers believe gentling improved Jack’s welfare at the shelter and saved his life. According to Morris Animal Foundation, “He and thousands like him are usually considered non-adoptable and euthanized within a few days of entering the shelter.”5

Gourkow and Phillips plan to continue their research into gentling by looking next at which methods are most effective. item.title: That Little Click Could Be a Big Clue
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Teeth chattering in dogs is exactly what it sounds like — the mouth opens and closes in quick succession, causing a soft clicking sound
  • The most familiar trigger is cold, where shivering muscles spill into the jaw — but persistent chattering after cold exposure can be a warning sign of hypothermia, which becomes a life-threatening emergency without prompt warming and veterinary care
  • Excitement, anticipation, and anxiety can all produce chattering too, and the body language tells you which is which
  • One of the most important causes to know about is oral or dental pain — periodontal disease, fractured teeth, abscesses, TMJ trouble, or oral growths can all cause chattering
  • Chattering can also signal gastrointestinal issues like nausea or reflux, ear infections, the flehmen response to pheromones, or even focal seizures

You hear it before you see it. A soft, fast clicking sound coming from your dog. You look over and there they are, mouth slightly open, teeth rapidly clacking together like they just stepped out of a cold pool. Maybe they are excited about a treat. Maybe it is chilly. Maybe nothing is going on at all. Or maybe something is.

Teeth chattering in dogs has a surprisingly wide range of possible meanings. Some are completely benign. Others are a quiet flag that something needs attention. Knowing how to tell them apart is one of those small skills that can make a real difference in your dog's day-to-day comfort. 

What Teeth Chattering Actually Looks Like

 Teeth chattering is exactly what it sounds like. Your dog opens and closes their mouth in quick succession, which causes the teeth to click together. It can be a few seconds of soft clicking or a more sustained rattling. Sometimes you will hear it. Other times you will mostly see the rapid jaw movement. 

It often happens alone but can be paired with shivering, drooling, head shaking, or other body-language signals. The trick to reading it is to look at everything happening around the chattering, not just the chattering itself.1,2

The Cold Response

This is probably the version most pet parents recognize. Just like in humans, shivering is the body's way of generating heat by rapidly contracting and relaxing muscles. When those muscle contractions involve the jaw, you get teeth chattering.

 How much cold a dog can tolerate depends on size, breed, coat, age, body condition, and how acclimated they are to the weather. Sighthounds with thin coats and little body fat may chatter at temperatures a double-coated sled dog would not even notice.

 Teeth chattering alone is not dangerous, but it is worth taking seriously. If your dog has been outside in the cold and you notice chattering, get them warm. Persistent cold exposure can tip into hypothermia, which is a life-threatening emergency.

Warning signs that chattering has crossed into hypothermia include an increased heart rate that then slows, rapid breathing followed by shallow breathing, confusion, lethargy, dilated pupils, and loss of consciousness. If you see any of these, your dog needs same-day veterinary care.3,4

Excitement and Anticipation

Sometimes the chattering is pure enthusiasm. A treat is being unwrapped. A favorite person walks through the door. The squirrel is on the deck again. The body's heightened emotional response can spill into the jaw, and the teeth start clicking.

Excited chattering is usually accompanied by upbeat body language — a raised or wagging tail, perked ears, a forward lean, eyes locked on whatever has captured their attention. It tends to stop the moment the trigger arrives (or leaves).5,6

Anxiety and Fear

Stress can lead to teeth chattering too, especially in situations a dog finds overwhelming. Veterinary visits are a common trigger. Greyhounds in particular often chatter during routine exams simply because they are nervous.7

The body language paints a different picture from the excited version. Anxious chattering usually comes with a tucked tail, flattened or pinned-back ears, lip licking, yawning, avoidance of eye contact, panting, or trembling. Some dogs pace, bark, or lunge.8

For hunting dogs, loud noises like gunshots or whistles can trigger an anxiety-driven response. The chattering usually stops once the stressor is gone, but repeated exposure to scary triggers without support can wear a dog down over time.9

Dental and Oral Pain

This is one of the most important causes to know about, because it is both common and easy to miss. Teeth chattering — especially when it happens regularly or without an obvious trigger — is often tied to pain in the mouth.10,11

Possible culprits include periodontal disease, fractured teeth, tooth root abscesses, tooth resorption, gum inflammation, and oral ulcers. Benign or cancerous growths in the mouth can also cause enough discomfort to produce chattering. Look for accompanying signs of dental trouble. These include:12,13,14

  • Bad breath
  • Drooling, sometimes with blood
  • Trouble picking up or chewing food
  • Chewing only on one side of the mouth
  • Preferring soft food over kibble or hard chews
  • Pawing at the mouth
  • Loss of appetite or unexplained weight loss
  • Visible swelling around the jaw

If any of these show up with the chattering, it is a veterinary conversation. A dental exam — sometimes with dental radiographs (X-rays) — is usually what gets to the bottom of it.

TMJ and Jaw Joint Trouble

The temporomandibular joint is the hinge that connects the upper and lower jaw. When it gets sore, fractured, or arthritic, dogs can chatter their teeth as a pain response.

Your veterinarian may gently open and close your dog's mouth to feel for resistance, grinding, or asymmetry. If TMJ disease is suspected, imaging like dental radiographs (X-rays) or a CT scan can help confirm what is going on.15,16,17

Gastrointestinal Issues

Stomach trouble is another less obvious cause. Dogs with nausea, vomiting, acid reflux, or stomach ulcers may grind or chatter their teeth. A clenched jaw rubbing back and forth produces a similar clicking sound, and drooling often goes along with it.

If chattering shows up around mealtimes, after eating, or alongside other GI signs like vomiting, drooling, or appetite changes, mention it to your veterinarian. Lab work, ultrasound, or endoscopy may be part of the workup.18

The Flehmen Response

This one is more curious than concerning. After sniffing another dog's scent — particularly when there is a hormonal angle, like an intact male sniffing where a female has been — some dogs will chatter their teeth and produce foamy saliva.

It is a form of the flehmen response. The chattering helps move scent molecules into the vomeronasal organ on the roof of the mouth, which specializes in detecting pheromones. It is a quirky bit of canine biology and not a problem.19

Seizures and Neurological Causes

Less commonly, teeth chattering can be a sign of a focal seizure — a seizure that affects only one part of the brain and may produce limited body movements rather than the dramatic shaking of a full grand mal seizure.

A key difference is responsiveness. A dog having a focal seizure usually will not respond to their name, will not look at you when you call, and may seem mentally absent during the episode. They may pace or seem clingy beforehand, and feel tired afterward.

If you suspect seizure activity, try to capture a short video and write down the timing and circumstances. Your veterinarian will use that information to decide whether to pursue neurological testing. White Shaker Dog Syndrome20 — a rare condition seen mostly in small white dogs — can also include teeth chattering.21,22,23

Other Possibilities to Keep in Mind

A few less common causes round out the list. Ear infections can produce enough pain to cause chattering. Inflamed jaw or facial muscles can do the same. Older dogs may chatter from cold sensitivity tied to low thyroid function, which is worth checking with a simple blood test.

And some dog behavior medications list teeth chattering as a possible side effect, so if it started after a new prescription, tell your veterinarian.

When to Call the Vet

Brief, situational chattering — your dog is cold, excited, or just smelled something fascinating — usually is not a problem. The pattern that calls for a veterinary visit looks different. Bring it up if you see:

  • Chattering that happens at rest, with no obvious trigger
  • Chattering paired with bad breath, drooling, bleeding, or swelling near the mouth
  • Trouble eating, weight loss, or appetite changes
  • Lethargy or signs of pain anywhere in the body
  • Chattering that started after a new medication
  • Episodes where your dog seems to space out or does not respond to their name
  • Hypothermia warning signs after cold exposure

A short video can be a huge help. Showing your veterinarian exactly what the chattering looks like — and what your dog is doing before and after — often shortens the path to a diagnosis.

What You Can Do at Home

Once medical causes have been ruled out or addressed, a few simple steps can reduce the chattering that is tied to environment or emotion. Coats, sweaters, heated beds, and shorter winter walks help cold-sensitive dogs stay comfortable. Daily tooth brushing with a dog-safe enzymatic toothpaste, plus routine dental checkups, can prevent the kind of oral pain that leads to chattering in the first place.

For anxiety-driven chattering, the goal is to give your dog space and slowly change how they feel about the trigger. Desensitization and counterconditioning — paired with the help of a certified behaviorist when needed — can go a long way. Calming pressure shirts, pheromone products, and supplements may help in specific situations, ideally with your veterinarian's input.

Read the Pattern, Not Just the Sound

That tiny clicking sound coming from your dog is rarely random. It might be a chilly morning. It might be the thrill of a treat. It might also be the only outward sign of a sore tooth, a stomach that does not feel right, or a stressful afternoon.

Pay attention to the pattern, not just the sound. If the chattering fits the moment and stops when the moment ends, you can usually take it at face value. If it shows up out of nowhere, sticks around, or comes with other changes, treat that little click like the clue it is — and let your vet help you decode it.

  • 2,3,5,8,14,16,22 American Kennel Club, February 26, 2026
  • 7,10,13,15,18,19,21 PetMD, February 4, 2025
  • 11 Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association, Volume 262: Issue 10, Page(s): 1363–1369, October 1, 2024

item.title: Poison Dart Frogs Lose Their Toxicity When Raised in Captivity
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Poison dart frogs secrete poison from their skin that can kill small animals and even an adult human
  • The poison comes from the frogs’ diet of toxic alkaloid-containing insects
  • When raised in captivity, the frogs aren’t fed these toxic insects, therefore lose their source of poisonous venom and eventually turn harmless (or are never harmless to begin with)
  • Wild poison dart frogs in disturbed habitats carry as few as 12 alkaloids compared to 30 in pristine forests, making them significantly less toxic
  • Venom from poison dart frogs has been used to develop a painkilling compound, and additional medicinal uses are being explored

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published June 7, 2016.

Poison dart frogs, also called poison arrow frogs, are known for two things — their striking appearance and their poisonous venom. The two go hand-in-hand, as the frogs' brilliant colors serve as a warning of their extreme toxicity.

One species, the golden poison dart frog, is only 2 inches long but contains enough venom to kill 10 people.1 It's said that even holding one in your hand could be fatal.2 The venom's deadly effects were well known to the indigenous Emberá people of Colombia, who coated the tips of their blowgun darts with the poisonous substance.

A curious feature about the frogs, however, is that while they're formidable poisonous creatures in nature, they tend to lose their toxicity when raised in captivity.

Poison Dart Frogs Raised in Captivity May Lose Their Poison

The reason why poison dart frogs raised in captivity tend to lose their poisonous venom is attributed to changes in their diet. The poison is not produced in the frogs, but rather comes from their diet and is then secreted from their skin.

In the wild, poison dart frogs feast on certain ants and beetles that contain toxic steroidal alkaloid molecules (which they either produce themselves or acquire via plants they eat). These toxins are responsible for the poison's toxic effects. They affect the nerves and muscles, leading to cardiac arrhythmia and heart failure.

When the frogs eat the ants or beetles,3 they store the toxic alkaloids in their glands and then secrete it as needed.

Valerie C. Clark, Ph.D. a then graduate student in chemistry at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York, authored a study in 2005 that identified some of the alkaloid-containing insects consumed by poison frogs.4 She told National Geographic:5

"It's really smart for frogs … It gives them a nice defense, and they don't have to waste energy biosynthesizing and making [the toxins] on their own …
And they're stealing it from their diet, which means they are also able to eat toxic insects other frogs reject as distasteful … They're able to exploit a whole other niche."

When raised in captivity, however, the frogs aren't fed these toxic insects, instead munching on non-alkaloid fruit flies, mealworms, crickets and termites. They therefore lose their source of poisonous venom and eventually turn harmless.

Are Wild Poison Frogs Losing Their Toxic Edge?

Separate research conducted by Clark and colleagues found even wild poison frogs may be losing some of their toxicity. Frogs with a greater diversity of alkaloids in their skin are generally most lethal to predators. However, the researchers found different make-ups of alkaloids in frogs from different regions.

Specifically, frogs from pristine forest areas had about 30 different alkaloids in their skin while those living in disturbed habitat had only about 12.

Even those living near a roadside in a moderately disturbed habitat had only 15 different alkaloids on average.6 Writing in the Journal of Chemical Ecology, the researchers noted:7

"… [F]rogs from the most pristine locality had the greatest number of alkaloids, whereas individuals from the most disturbed localities had the least.
In a comparison of frog alkaloid profiles over a 10- to 14-year period, alkaloid turnover, and thus presumably alkaloid-source arthropod turnover, was high in a disturbed locality and low in the pristine primary forest locality."

The reduction in alkaloid variety is likely due to a reduction in arthropod species (insects) in the frogs' diets.

Poison Frog Fun Facts

Poison dart frogs can live from 3 to 15 years in the wild, a lengthy lifespan that's attributed largely to their lack of predators. The only known natural predator of these frogs is a snake called Leimadophis epinephelus, which is resistant to their poison.8

The frogs have an elaborate mating ritual, which includes male frogs vocalizing to attract females. The females deposit eggs on leaves and the males check on the eggs for two weeks until the tadpoles hatch.

At this point, the male carries the tadpoles on his back (held in place via a mucus secretion) and takes them to a watery spot to continue development. This includes small ponds, water collected in coconut shells or even water inside a bromeliad plant.

The tadpoles are then left on their own to develop into frogs (a process that takes about three months). If researchers are correct and wild frogs continue to become less toxic due to habitat disturbances, it's possible that other species could catch on and start to prey upon the newly defenseless frogs.

This could have dramatic ramifications for the surrounding ecosystems as well as impact their medicinal uses. Venom from poison dart frogs has been used to develop a compound that might act as a painkiller in humans and other medical uses for the venom are also being explored.

If you opt to keep amphibians as pets please only buy ethically raised, captive-bred specimens. Purchasing wild-caught animals contributes to ecologic decline and these animals often die in captivity from stress.

Sources and References

  • Today I Found Out February 12, 2016
  • 1,8 National Geographic, Poison Dart Frogs
  • 2 Mongabay August 9, 2005
  • 3 PNAS November 1, 2004
  • 4 PNAS August 8, 2005
  • 5,6 National Geographic November 6, 2006 (Archived)
  • 7 J Chem Ecol. 2006 Oct;32(10):2219-3

  • When raised in captivity, the frogs aren’t fed these toxic insects, therefore lose their source of poisonous venom and eventually turn harmless (or are never harmless to begin with)
  • Wild poison dart frogs in disturbed habitats carry as few as 12 alkaloids compared to 30 in pristine forests, making them significantly less toxic
  • Venom from poison dart frogs has been used to develop a painkilling compound, and additional medicinal uses are being explored

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published June 7, 2016.

Poison dart frogs, also called poison arrow frogs, are known for two things — their striking appearance and their poisonous venom. The two go hand-in-hand, as the frogs' brilliant colors serve as a warning of their extreme toxicity.

One species, the golden poison dart frog, is only 2 inches long but contains enough venom to kill 10 people.1 It's said that even holding one in your hand could be fatal.2 The venom's deadly effects were well known to the indigenous Emberá people of Colombia, who coated the tips of their blowgun darts with the poisonous substance.

A curious feature about the frogs, however, is that while they're formidable poisonous creatures in nature, they tend to lose their toxicity when raised in captivity.

Poison Dart Frogs Raised in Captivity May Lose Their Poison

The reason why poison dart frogs raised in captivity tend to lose their poisonous venom is attributed to changes in their diet. The poison is not produced in the frogs, but rather comes from their diet and is then secreted from their skin.

In the wild, poison dart frogs feast on certain ants and beetles that contain toxic steroidal alkaloid molecules (which they either produce themselves or acquire via plants they eat). These toxins are responsible for the poison's toxic effects. They affect the nerves and muscles, leading to cardiac arrhythmia and heart failure.

When the frogs eat the ants or beetles,3 they store the toxic alkaloids in their glands and then secrete it as needed.

Valerie C. Clark, Ph.D. a then graduate student in chemistry at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York, authored a study in 2005 that identified some of the alkaloid-containing insects consumed by poison frogs.4 She told National Geographic:5

"It's really smart for frogs … It gives them a nice defense, and they don't have to waste energy biosynthesizing and making [the toxins] on their own …
And they're stealing it from their diet, which means they are also able to eat toxic insects other frogs reject as distasteful … They're able to exploit a whole other niche."

When raised in captivity, however, the frogs aren't fed these toxic insects, instead munching on non-alkaloid fruit flies, mealworms, crickets and termites. They therefore lose their source of poisonous venom and eventually turn harmless.

Are Wild Poison Frogs Losing Their Toxic Edge?

Separate research conducted by Clark and colleagues found even wild poison frogs may be losing some of their toxicity. Frogs with a greater diversity of alkaloids in their skin are generally most lethal to predators. However, the researchers found different make-ups of alkaloids in frogs from different regions.

Specifically, frogs from pristine forest areas had about 30 different alkaloids in their skin while those living in disturbed habitat had only about 12.

Even those living near a roadside in a moderately disturbed habitat had only 15 different alkaloids on average.6 Writing in the Journal of Chemical Ecology, the researchers noted:7

"… [F]rogs from the most pristine locality had the greatest number of alkaloids, whereas individuals from the most disturbed localities had the least.
In a comparison of frog alkaloid profiles over a 10- to 14-year period, alkaloid turnover, and thus presumably alkaloid-source arthropod turnover, was high in a disturbed locality and low in the pristine primary forest locality."

The reduction in alkaloid variety is likely due to a reduction in arthropod species (insects) in the frogs' diets.

Poison Frog Fun Facts

Poison dart frogs can live from 3 to 15 years in the wild, a lengthy lifespan that's attributed largely to their lack of predators. The only known natural predator of these frogs is a snake called Leimadophis epinephelus, which is resistant to their poison.8

The frogs have an elaborate mating ritual, which includes male frogs vocalizing to attract females. The females deposit eggs on leaves and the males check on the eggs for two weeks until the tadpoles hatch.

At this point, the male carries the tadpoles on his back (held in place via a mucus secretion) and takes them to a watery spot to continue development. This includes small ponds, water collected in coconut shells or even water inside a bromeliad plant.

The tadpoles are then left on their own to develop into frogs (a process that takes about three months). If researchers are correct and wild frogs continue to become less toxic due to habitat disturbances, it's possible that other species could catch on and start to prey upon the newly defenseless frogs.

This could have dramatic ramifications for the surrounding ecosystems as well as impact their medicinal uses. Venom from poison dart frogs has been used to develop a compound that might act as a painkiller in humans and other medical uses for the venom are also being explored.

If you opt to keep amphibians as pets please only buy ethically raised, captive-bred specimens. Purchasing wild-caught animals contributes to ecologic decline and these animals often die in captivity from stress.

item.title: This Fruit Has a Reputation Problem
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Most dogs and cats won’t be interested in eating grapefruit, but it’s safe for them to consume, if they show an interest
  • Offer grapefruit to your pets with the peel and seeds removed, portioned into bite-sized pieces that your pet can comfortably chew
  • Naringin and naringenin are the primary bioactive polyphenols in citrus fruits; they exhibit anticancer properties and protective action against diabetes, neurodegeneration, metabolic syndrome and cardiovascular disorders
  • Red grapefruits are considered one of the important sources of lycopene, which has antioxidant, antihypertensive, neuroprotective, cardioprotective and anti-inflammatory properties
  • Look for grapefruits that have a deeper color without green patches, as this indicates ripeness. Having an oval shape or a flat side is also an indicator that they’ve softened up and have become sweeter

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published April 14, 2023.

Grapefruit (Citrus × paradisi) is a fairly new addition to the citrus family, believed to have originated from the island of Barbados as a result of hybridization between a sweet orange and a pomelo.1,2 It’s one of the larger citrus fruits, with a diameter of 10 to 15 centimeters (4 to 6 inches). It has a thick, smooth rind that’s yellow or pink-blushed, with a red, pink or white flesh that tastes sweet, tart and mildly bitter.3,4 It grows in clusters on trees, similar to grapes, hence its name.5

Grapefruit is eaten peeled and raw, the same way you would eat an orange, clementine or any other citrus fruit. It can also be juiced or used in salads and sweet or savory dishes, as it pairs well with fish and pork.6 But can pets also enjoy this fruit and benefit from it the same way you do? Continue reading to find out.

Top U.S. Producers of Grapefruit

The U.S. is a principal exporter of grapefruit. Florida leads the production, harvesting 3.3 million boxes of grapefruit during the 2021 to 2022 season,7 while California and Texas came in at 2nd and 3rd place.8

The Lowdown on Grapefruit’s Safety for Pets

Misinformation about many healthy fruits, vegetables, nuts and seeds abounds on the internet. This is because websites have labeled all risks (such as the risk of overconsumption causing gastrointestinal issues, as is the case with grapefruit) as "toxicities," which isn't true but has managed to confuse millions of pet lovers, nonetheless.

In the case of grapefruit, there’s confusion among pet parents whether it’s safe to share with pets or not, as some websites say grapefruit is toxic to cats and dogs. However, there are no cited sources for the claims that the fruit is toxic. Grapefruit flesh has no published toxicity reports and can be safely offered to pets as a healthy snack, which constitutes less than 10% of your pet’s overall calories.

It’s the peel and other plant parts that contain essential oils, which can cause stomach discomfort and have been associated with adverse events. Hence, you can easily avoid adverse effects by offering your pet only the flesh of the grapefruit and making sure they don’t have access to any discarded peels or other plant parts.

“Offer grapefruit to your pets the same way you would eat it — with the peel and seeds removed, portioned into slices or bite-sized pieces that your pet can comfortably chew.”

Cats, in general, have an aversion to citrus fruits, but it’s safe to offer them a bite of peeled grapefruit if they’re interested in eating some. The citric acid in the flesh can cause loose stools when consumed in excess, so remember not to offer your pet too many slices.9,10 Relatedly, keep in mind that healthy treats like this should make up less than 10% of your pet’s daily caloric intake, and always start by offering only tiny amounts.

Dogs often aren’t interested in trying grapefruit, but if your dog is, always start with a piece that’s half the size of one paw, and make sure that it doesn’t cause loose stools. If your pup has no stool changes, you can slowly increase the amounts you offer.

Naringin and Naringenin — Anticancer Polyphenols in Grapefruit

Naringin and its aglycone form naringenin are the primary bioactive polyphenols in citrus fruits. Naringenin is particularly high in grapefruit extract at 43.5 milligrams per 100-milliliter serving.11 According to a study published in the journal Biomedicines:12

“Numerous studies have reported these substances’ antioxidant and antiandrogenic properties, as well as their ability to protect from inflammation and cancer, in various in vitro and in vivo experimental models in animals and humans.”

These compounds have been shown to interfere with cancer development and progression through various mechanisms of action, including “modulating several unregulated signaling pathways associated with inflammation, proliferation, apoptosis, autophagy, angiogenesis, invasion and metastasis.”13

In addition to their anticancer properties, naringin and naringenin have also been found to exhibit protective action against diabetes, neurodegeneration, metabolic syndrome and cardiovascular disorders.14,15

Red and Pink Grapefruits Provide Lycopene and Beta-Carotene

Lycopene is a type of carotenoid that exhibits powerful antioxidant properties. It’s found in red, pink and orange fruits and vegetables. Red grapefruits, in particular, are considered one of the important sources of this compound,16 although it’s also found in the pink varieties.17 In addition to the ability to fight free radicals, lycopene also exhibits antihypertensive, neuroprotective, cardioprotective and anti-inflammatory properties.18

Studies have also documented lycopene’s anticancer action. In a study published in the American Journal of Veterinary Research, researchers evaluated the effects of lycopene on the growth and death of canine osteosarcoma cells. Their findings showed lycopene alone helped cause “mild to pronounced” reduction in the proliferation of cancer cells, as well as apoptosis (cell death) in highly metastasizing canine osteosarcoma cell lines.19

Another powerful antioxidant carotenoid found in red and pink grapefruits is beta-carotene (provitamin A).20 A 100-gram serving of pink or red grapefruit provides 686 micrograms of this compound.21 Research has shown that beta-carotene may help improve canine immune responses, particularly in older dogs.22 Another study published in the Journal of Nutritional Science also found that beta-carotene helped improve retinal response and reduced age-related retinal and visual functional decline in dogs.23

Did You Know?

Red grapefruit gets its color from high amounts of lycopene,24 and research shows grapefruits grown in shade have a more intense red hue than those exposed to light.25

Other Beneficial Nutrients Found in Grapefruit

Another major bioactive compound found in grapefruit is hesperidin, which has antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antiviral and anticancer properties, and may help protect against cardiovascular and neurodegenerative disorders.26 A study in Research in Veterinary Science noted hesperidin to be one of the “promising candidates to be considered in the treatment of CDV (canine distemper virus),” as it exhibited antiviral activity against it.27

Grapefruit is also rich in vitamin C, providing 31.2 milligrams per 100-gram servings.28 Although dogs can synthesize vitamin C in their body, getting supplementary amounts of this vitamin from their diet can be good for their health. Vitamin C is a powerful antioxidant, helping reduce inflammation and cognitive decline.29 It also plays an important role in the biosynthesis of collagen, L-carnitine and certain neurotransmitters.30

Is Growing Grapefruit Sustainable?

Grapefruit farming is considered sustainable, as it does not have significant impact on air, water, soil and other resources.31 In Florida, grapefruit growers have been using sustainable farming practices to reduce water usage, limit erosion and reduce pesticide use, such as using red kaolin clay to repel insects.32


With that said, grapefruit ranks No. 21 in the Environmental Working Group’s Shopper’s Guide to Pesticides in Produce™,33 which means that conventionally grown varieties may still have traces of pesticides even though they’re not the most heavily contaminated.


For this reason, opt to buy organic, spray-free grapefruit from your local farmers market as much as possible. If you only have conventionally grown grapefruit, wash it well before peeling.

How to Choose Grapefruit and Offer It to Your Pets

When choosing grapefruits for your family, aside from opting for organic whenever possible, you should also look for grapefruits that have a deeper color without green patches, as this indicates ripeness. Having an oval shape or a flat side is also an indicator that they’ve softened up and have become sweeter. They should also feel plump and heavy for their size, with a smooth rind that gives slightly but bounces back after you give it a gentle squeeze.34,35

As mentioned earlier, peel the rind of the grapefruit before serving it fresh to your pet as a snack or using it as an ingredient in a homemade training treat. You can put any leftover peeled sections in an airtight container and store it in the refrigerator.36

Pureed and frozen grapefruit can be a refreshing snack for pets too, especially during the warmer months. You can mix it with other mashed or soft foods (like plain yogurt and squash), and spread it on their lick mat — this also helps mask the tart flavor of the grapefruit, which some pets may find off-putting.

As with other fruits, grapefruit contains sugar, which can harm your pet’s health when consumed in excessive amounts, so remember not to give them too much of this fruit. Avoid giving your pet grapefruit-flavored food or drinks as well, as they’re often loaded with added sugars and high-fructose corn syrup.

item.title: Definitely Not the Long-Term Death Sentence You May Think It Is
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • The most common type of arthritis in dogs is osteoarthritis (OA), also known as degenerative joint disease
  • Osteoarthritis can be a primary disease associated with aging, or secondary disease with a wide range of causes
  • Three persistent myths about OA are that it occurs only in old dogs, that dogs with the condition should not exercise and that OA is a long-term death sentence
  • Dogs with OA can live long, good-quality lives when they are kept lean and well-conditioned, receive an individualized treatment protocol and are monitored regularly for mobility and comfort
  • In arthritic dogs, an average weight loss of just 9% resulted in 82% of dogs showing measurable improvement in lameness

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published September 13, 2017.

There are several different forms of arthritis that occur in dogs, but by far the most common is osteoarthritis (OA), also known as degenerative joint disease (DJD) or degenerative arthritis. This type of arthritis causes progressive, long-term, permanent deterioration of the cartilage surrounding the joints.

OA can be a primary or secondary disease. Symptoms of primary osteoarthritis typically occur as part of the aging process. Secondary OA, on the other hand, can have a wide range of causes, including trauma, abnormal wear and tear on the joints and cartilage or an inherited defect present at birth such as hip dysplasia. Additional causes of secondary OA include:

  • Abnormal development of joints, commonly the hip or elbow (exacerbated by irregular growth and development, as well as vaccine reactions)
  • Dislocation of the kneecap or subluxation of the kneecap or shoulder
  • Osteochondrosis dissecans (OCD), a condition in which a flap of cartilage develops abnormally within the joint
  • Obesity, which increases stress on the joints
  • Diabetes
  • Prolonged steroid therapy
  • Excessive laxity (looseness) of the joints

Symptoms of osteoarthritis vary and include reduced activity level, occasional lameness and a stiff gait that gets worse after exercise, long periods of activity and in cold weather.

Myths About Osteoarthritis

According to veterinary surgeon and rehabilitation specialist Dr. Denis Marcellin-Little, writing for veterinary journal dvm360, there are three common misconceptions about OA:1

  • Myth No. 1 — Osteoarthritis only affects older dogs — Many people don't realize that OA has more to do with genetics and a dog's development than normal wear and tear on the joints of the body. In fact, joint degeneration often begins as puppies experience a rapid growth spurt during the first 4 to 6 months of life.

    "Although it's present early on," says Marcellin-Little, "it tends to pass under the radar for years and be diagnosed only when its impact is much more profound later in life."


    Feeding a nutritionally balanced diet that meets FEDIAF (the European Pet Food Industry Federation — the European equivalent to AAFCO) standards for large breed puppies (early and late growth) is recommended because those standards are more appropriate for large and giant breeds.
  • Myth No. 2 — Dogs with OA shouldn't be physically active — Actually, the opposite is true. Exercise is tremendously important in helping dogs forestall progression of the disease. Studies show that people with OA who exercise regularly are less depressed, less anxious, need fewer drugs and function and feel better. The same is true for dogs.
  • Myth No. 3 — OA is a long-term death sentence — Dogs with degenerative joint disease can enjoy long, full, good-quality lives when their condition is diagnosed early and managed effectively. This absolutely includes keeping them active and well-conditioned. It's also important to regularly monitor the mobility and comfort of your dog's joints so that her treatment protocol can be adjusted as needed.

A Lean Weight and Good Muscle Tone Are Crucial for Dogs with OA

Arthritic dogs who are also overweight or obese have a much more difficult time with pain and mobility than lean animals, and in addition, it's important to know that overfeeding puppies may play a role in causing OA.

item.title: The Secret Behind Your Dog's Dramatic Sigh
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Sighing in dogs is real, normal, and often meaningful — it is a deeper inhale followed by a slow exhale that brings in extra oxygen, expels carbon dioxide, and helps reset tiny air sacs in the lungs called alveoli
  • The most common reasons dogs sigh includes contentment and relaxation (often paired with a soft face and loose body), pleasure during petting, boredom or frustration, disappointment when something fun ends, and attention seeking
  • A sigh in a tense or unfamiliar setting can be a self-soothing response to anxiety, especially if paired with a tucked tail, flat ears, lip licking, yawning, trembling, or pacing
  • Some sounds that look or sound like sighs actually point to bigger problems: moans can indicate pain, labored breathing involves visible effort with each breath, panting at rest can signal heat or heart issues, and wheezing can mean a blocked airway
  • Occasional sighing is part of normal dog life, but a sudden increase in sighing or sighing paired with changes in appetite, energy, posture, or breathing rate (a healthy dog rests at about 15 to 30 breaths per minute) is worth a quick check-in with your vet

Your dog curls up next to you on the couch, gets comfortable, and lets out a sigh so deep and theatrical it sounds like they have had the longest day of their life. Or they are staring at you from across the room while you finish an email, and you hear that pointed little exhale that feels suspiciously like commentary.

If it sometimes seems like your dog is sighing on purpose, you are not imagining things. Sighing is real, it is normal, and it can mean a surprising number of things depending on the moment. The trick is learning to read the context.

What a Sigh Actually Is

A sigh is a deeper, longer breath than the rhythmic ones your dog takes all day. It usually starts with an audible inhale that runs about twice the length of a normal breath, followed by a slow, pronounced exhale. Sometimes it comes out through the mouth. More often, in dogs, it comes out through the nose with the mouth closed.1

Physiologically, sighing brings in extra oxygen and helps move carbon dioxide out. It is a quiet reset for the respiratory system, and it is something every mammal does. The dramatic version is the one we notice, but plenty of sighs are subtle enough that we miss them entirely.2,3

Sighing Is a Built-In Reflex

Before we get to the emotional reasons, it helps to know that sighing is partly just biology. Dogs (and humans) sigh several times an hour without thinking about it, because those occasional deep breaths help keep the lungs working properly.4

Tiny air sacs in the lungs called alveoli can collapse if they are not stretched open from time to time. A sigh inflates them again, almost like resetting a balloon that has gotten a little floppy. This is happening in the background all day, whether your dog is napping, walking, or staring out the window.5,6

So, a sigh, by itself, is rarely something to read too much into. It is the context around the sigh — the body language, the situation, the timing — that tells the real story.

Sighing May Be a Sign of Contentment and Relaxation

This is probably the version most pet parents recognize. Your dog flops onto their bed, gets settled, and the sigh just rolls out. They are comfortable. They are letting go. They are signaling to their own body, and to you, that everything is okay.

A contented sigh in moments of relaxation is paired with a soft face; closed or half-closed eyes, loose ears and a relaxed tail and body. The mouth may be slightly open and there is no tension present.7,8

Senior dogs especially seem to sigh as they finally find the right position to settle into, which can be a sign that the spot they have chosen feels good. Puppies do their own version too — sometimes a soft sigh, sometimes a tiny groan that means much the same thing.9

Pets Also Sigh During Petting or Play

That sigh you get during a long belly rub, or a slow ear scratch is a close cousin of the contentment sigh. It is your dog telling you that the moment is hitting the spot.

Again, look for that calm body language — a soft face, half-closed eyes, relaxed posture, a loose tail. If your dog leans in, exhales deeply, and stays in place, the sigh is almost certainly a happy one. Learning to read your pet’s body language is one of the most useful skills a pet parent can develop.10

Bored or Frustrated Pets Sigh, Too

Now we move into the more pointed sighs. If you are deep into a work project and your dog is across the room watching you, the sigh you hear might be the canine equivalent of an eye roll. Sometimes this type of sigh can also sound more like a “huff.”

A bored sigh tends to come with alert, open eyes and a body that looks anxious or anticipatory rather than relaxed. Your dog may shift positions, glance at the door, or rest their chin on their paws and stare. The sigh is saying, plainly, "this is not very interesting" or “come on, let’s do something fun.”

Active dogs stuck inside on rainy days are especially prone to sighing out their frustration. A walk, a tug session, a puzzle toy, or a few minutes of indoor training can usually turn that around.

It Can Also Be a Sign of Disappointment

Some dogs sigh when something good comes to an end — the walk is over, the toy is being put away, and the visitor is leaving. The body language looks a lot like the bored sigh: alert eyes, a watchful posture, sometimes a head resting heavily on the floor or a paw.

It is hard to know exactly how much of this is intentional and how much is the body releasing tension as the fun winds down. Either way, it is a sweet, slightly theatrical part of living with a dog who really did love what just happened.

Your Dog May Be Seeking Attention

Dogs are sharper than we give them credit for. If a sigh has ever resulted in you looking up, putting your phone down, or saying "what is it, buddy?” your dog has noticed. Some dogs learn that a well-timed sigh gets a response, and they start using it that way.

This is a pretty harmless habit, and arguably preferable to other attention-getting strategies like chewing the rug or excessive barking. If your dog has trained you to look over when they sigh, well, congratulations to them.

Anxiety or Stress Can Also Trigger a Sigh

A sigh in the waiting room at the vet's office is not the same kind of sigh as the one on the couch. In a tense or unfamiliar environment, sighing can be a sign your dog is trying to self-soothe.

Deep breathing can help dial down stress, and dogs use it the same way we do. The body language will look different from a contented sigh — you may see a tucked tail, ears flat against the head, lip licking, yawning, trembling, pacing, or hypervigilance (when your dog seems on guard even when nothing is actually wrong).

If sighing is paired with these stress signals, the kindest thing you can do is reduce the pressure of the situation — move away from whatever is causing it, give your dog a quiet spot, or work with a trainer on desensitization techniques over time.

Sighing Is Common When a Pet Is in Pain or Discomfort

Sighing is not a classic sign of pain in dogs, but it can sometimes accompany it — especially in senior dogs or dogs with arthritis who are working to find a comfortable position. The sigh you hear when they finally settle down might be relief.

Other signs that a sigh might be tied to discomfort include limping, restlessness, panting at rest, withdrawal from interaction, changes in eating or sleeping or signs of pain such as whimpering or wincing when touched. If you suspect that your pet is in pain, a veterinary exam is the right next step.

One useful tip: If your dog repeatedly sighs while you are cuddling them, sometimes that sigh is a polite version of "I have had enough now." Stiff body, ears that flatten, or an attempt to slide away can confirm it. Letting them have their space goes a long way.

When It Is Not Really a Sigh

A few dog sounds can look or sound like sighs at first glance but actually point to something different — and sometimes more serious. It is worth knowing the difference.11,12

  • Moans come from the vocal cords, not from a deep breath. They can indicate pain or discomfort — abdominal, back, or joint — and warrant a vet visit if they are new or frequent.
  • Panting is many short, rapid breaths rather than one long one. Normal panting cools dogs down or accompanies excitement but panting or breathing heavily at rest in room temperature, or combined with other symptoms such as coughing, lethargy, drooling, or vomiting is a reason to call your vet.
  • Labored breathing involves visible effort with each breath — the chest wall and abdomen (belly) will be working harder than usual with more effort each time they breathe. Unlike a single sigh, it is sustained. If your pet has labored breathing and especially if they are breathing rapidly with over thirty breaths in one minute — this is an emergency and you should see your vet as soon as possible.
  • Wheezing or a high-pitched whistle on breathing can mean a blocked or narrowed airway or a respiratory issue and also needs prompt veterinary attention.
  • Yawns also involve a big inhale, but the mouth opens wide, just like in people. A yawn here and there is normal in dogs; but yawning alongside lip licking, whale eye (the whites of the eyes showing), and a tense body can also mean stress or anxiety.

When to Check in with Your Vet

Occasional sighing is part of being a dog. But if your dog suddenly starts sighing much more than usual, or if sighing shows up with other changes — like rapid or noisy breathing, coughing, decreased appetite, low energy, or a change in behavior — a quick veterinary visit is a sensible step. New or unusual patterns are worth a closer look.

For reference, a healthy dog at rest takes somewhere around 15 to 30 breaths per minute (when they are not panting), with their chest rising and falling rhythmically. Anything that looks substantially different — especially fast breathing while at rest (over thirty breaths per minute); labored, or noisy breathing — deserves a phone call.13,14

Decoding a Sigh Is Easier Than You Think

That dramatic sigh from your dog is one of the most expressive sounds they make, and it almost always means something — even if that something is just a perfectly natural reflex. Most of the time, sighing is a happy, harmless part of dog life: a wind-down after a long walk, a satisfied response to a belly rub, a tiny editorial comment when you are taking too long with dinner.

The secret behind the dramatic sigh is mostly that it is not particularly mysterious. Read the room — the soft face, the alert eyes, the relaxed or tense body language — and you will usually know exactly what your dog is telling you. And on the off chance the sighing changes or comes with other red flags, your vet is the best partner for figuring out the rest.

Sources and References

  • 1,5,7,10,12,13 Chewy, April 30, 2025
  • 2,4,6,8 American Kennel Club, June 12, 2025
  • 3,9,11,14 PetMD, July 24, 2024

item.title: This Cat Understands Everything She Says
item.description:

item.title: This Misunderstood Farm Animal That's Playful Like a Dog
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Pigs share many cognitive, emotional and personality traits with animals that are considered to be intelligent, such as chimpanzees and dogs
  • Pigs can prioritize important memories, anticipate positive and negative situations, and display spatial learning skills, such as learning how to navigate a maze
  • Pigs demonstrate a form of empathy and are also playful animals, displaying many similar play behaviors as dogs
  • Play is critical to pigs' emotional and cognitive development — insufficient opportunity to explore leads to behavioral abnormalities
  • The Nonhuman Rights Project is petitioning courts to recognize that certain nonhuman animals, including great apes, elephants and dolphins, are entitled to basic legal rights

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published April 26, 2016.

Pigs are easily one of the most misunderstood animal species. They're viewed by many as dirty and useful for little more than a food source — but in fact they're highly intelligent (and among the cleanest domestic animals).

A report published in the International Journal of Comparative Psychology reviewed cognition, emotion and personality in pigs and revealed they share many traits with animals that are considered to be intelligent.1

The findings should have major implications for the industrial livestock industry, which raises pigs on CAFOs (concentrated animal feeding operations) as though they are non-thinking objects, not intelligent beings.

Unfortunately, while it's excellent news that pigs are starting to gain some much-needed recognition, it will likely be some time before the findings permeate through to the livestock industry.

Pigs Are Psychologically Complex Animals

Researchers from Emory University reviewed dozens of studies on pigs and other animals, revealing compelling insights that pigs are psychologically complex. For instance, pigs are highly social animals and use their snouts to engage in behaviors such as rooting, carrying and pushing, and social interactions.

Pigs can also prioritize important memories, such as which site typically contains more food, anticipate positive and negative situations, and display spatial learning skills, such as learning how to navigate a maze.

Pigs are also playful animals and display many similar play behaviors as dogs. Among them, pigs may carry or shake objects such as a ball or stick, toss straw into the air, run playfully, hop around, jump, paw and scamper. They may also engage in play fighting, pushing and running after each other.

Play, it turns out, is extremely important for pigs' emotional and cognitive development. According to the study:2

"So important is this need that insufficient opportunity to explore leads to behavioral abnormalities.
Young pigs reared in a cognitively challenging and complex environment affording greater interactions with objects and other pigs are more socio-cognitively developed than their counterparts raised in standard farrowing crates found that when given access to materials allowing for exploration, pigs engaged in more behaviors associated with positive affect, such as play, and especially locomotor play.
Also, consistent with these findings is the fact that pigs make more optimistic choices (have a positive bias) when in enriched environments than in others, indicating that they find stimulation rewarding and pleasurable.
Therefore, opportunities for play and exploration impact emotional development in pigs as well."

Pig Intelligence Rivals That of Dogs and Chimps

Study co-author and neuroscientist Lori Marino, Ph.D. of Emory University and The Nonhuman Rights Project said in a press release:

"We have shown that pigs share a number of cognitive capacities with other highly intelligent species such as dogs, chimpanzees, elephants, dolphins, and even humans … There is good scientific evidence to suggest we need to rethink our overall relationship to them."

Pigs, it appears, develop sophisticated social behaviors, including competitive behaviors, as seen in some primate species. They are also sensitive to the attentional state of humans, which is also seen in dogs and primates.

For instance, young pigs can utilize human head cues to discriminate between different attention states in humans. They prefer humans who are attentive, and can also distinguish between familiar and unfamiliar humans.

In addition, pigs may show empathy; they not only connect with the emotions of other pigs but also to do so with pigs who are responding emotionally in anticipation of future events. The researchers also revealed that pigs:3

  • Have excellent long-term memories
  • Excel at tests requiring location of objects
  • Comprehend a symbolic language
  • Learn complex combinations of symbols for actions and objects
  • Live in social communities and learn from one another
  • Cooperate with one another
  • Move a joystick to move an on-screen cursor (similar to chimpanzees)
  • Can use a mirror to find hidden food

Should Intelligent Animals Like Pigs Have Rights?

Research into the sentience of pigs raises some important ethical considerations. Most people would agree that chimpanzees, dogs and other intelligent creatures, like elephants and dolphins, deserve some form of protections and rights.

Yet, pigs, which appear to be similarly intelligent, are raised in some of the most inhumane conditions on the planet.

The Nonhuman Rights Project is tackling such issues head on; they're petitioning courts to recognize that existing scientific evidence suggests certain nonhuman animals are entitled to basic legal rights, including bodily liberty and integrity.

In December 2013, the organization filed lawsuits on behalf of four chimpanzees that are imprisoned in New York. The cases, which are moving through the appellate courts, call for the chimps to be freed and transferred to live on a sanctuary.

The group intends to first focus on rights for great apes, elephants, dolphins and whales, "for whom there is clear scientific evidence of such complex cognitive abilities as self-awareness and autonomy."4 It's not a stretch that someday pigs should also be granted some form of protection or at least the ability to live out their days engaging in natural pig behaviors that are currently impossible on CAFOs. It's intriguing work, and this is only the beginning.

Marino and colleagues have also found evidence of cognitive, emotional and social complexity in chickens, and they plan to study other CAFO animals, including cows and goats, in the near future.5

Sources and References

  • 1,2 International Journal of Comparative Psychology 2015, 28
  • 3,5 Discovery News June 11, 2015 (Archived)
  • 4 The Nonhuman Rights Project, Q&A (Archived)
