item.title: The Citrus Fruit Pet Parents Always Ask About
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Oranges are OK as dog treats, as they may provide nutrients like vitamin C, flavonoids and other bioactive compounds
  • The vitamin C in oranges may help boost immunity in pets and support collagen production, which is important for joint, skin and coat health
  • Oranges' phytochemical content, like saponins and tannins, may help curb inflammation
  • Feed your dogs a few fresh slices, obviously peeled with the seeds removed
  • Make sure you don’t give them the peel, since it may cause stomach discomfort due to the essential oils it contain

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published October 2, 2018.

Oranges are one of the most popular fruits in the U.S., ranking in 6th place behind bananas, strawberries, grapes, apples and watermelon.1 While this popularity may be all thanks to their taste and flavor, oranges are also well known for the nutrients they offer. These fruits contain a surplus of bioactive compounds and metabolites crucial for biological processes, such as immune function and collagen production.2

Most people enjoy eating fresh orange slices because of their sweet and refreshing flavor. However, if you suddenly notice your dog eyeing a piece or two, you may be curious if your pet can tolerate this fruit or not.

With its surplus of bioactive components, as well as the health benefits this fruit has to offer, small amounts of fresh oranges can be shared. Oranges can be given to pets as healthy treats (make sure all treats make up less than 10% of their daily caloric intake) or added to their nutritionally adequate, species-appropriate diet.

Where Do Oranges Grow?

Every year, about 50 million tons of oranges are harvested all around the world. While this fruit is cultivated in different regions, three countries lead the pack in orange production:3

1. Brazil — 15.9 million tons

2. China — 7.5 million tons

3. U.S. — 4.2 million tons

Protect Pets Against Pathogens with Oranges’ Phytochemicals

Researchers from the University of Benin and Kentucky published a study analyzing the phytochemical components of oranges. They found plentiful bioactive compounds, such as flavonoids, tannins, saponins and alkaloids, which lend oranges their antibacterial, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties.

Optimizing your pet’s diet to include these compounds may help protect them from infections and chronic diseases triggered by constant inflammation.4

Did You Know?

Oranges aren’t found in the wild naturally, since they’re a cross between two citrus fruits: pomelo and mandarin. Oranges got the best of their parent fruits, inheriting the sweetness of the mandarin and the fibrous flesh of the pomelo.5

Boost Your Pet’s Immune System with Vitamin C

"Vitamin C is often regarded as the most important vitamin found in citrus fruits. This antioxidant is linked to the immune system and iron absorption."

For its function in immunity, vitamin C works by boosting both the adaptive and innate immune systems. It is especially important in supporting the epithelial barrier function and skin health — the body’s first line of defense against pathogens.

Vitamin C also figures in collagen production, a component that is not only vital for wound healing and skin health, but is also responsible for decreasing gut permeability and improving microbiota health.6,7 Two tablespoons of orange slices can offer your pet up to 12 milligrams of vitamin C.8

Fun Fact About Oranges

Only 20% of all fruits, including oranges, produced worldwide are sold as fresh fruits. The remaining 80% are typically processed into juice, preserves and extracts.9

How to Feed Oranges to Pets

Remember that misinformation about many healthy fruits, vegetables, nuts and seeds abounds on the internet. This is because websites have labeled all risks (such as the risk of overconsumption causing gastrointestinal issues, or choking on too large of pieces or pits) as "toxicities," which isn't true but has managed to confuse millions of pet lovers, nonetheless.

As for oranges, you can safely feed your dogs a few fresh slices, obviously peeled with the seeds removed. Just make sure you don’t give them the peel, since it may cause stomach discomfort due to the essential oils it contains. Too many orange slices can cause loose stools if fed in excess. Cats generally have an aversion to all citrus, but a bite of orange is safe for cats (without the peel).

Orange-flavored food or drinks, such as orange juice and canned oranges, shouldn’t be given to pets, since they’re often loaded with added sugars and high-fructose corn syrups, and excessive sugar consumption can be problematic for pets, just as it can be for humans.10

Remember that while oranges and other fresh fruits are healthy, all "extras," including oranges, should be limited to only about 10% of your pet’s daily diet, together with other types of treats. Your pet should be getting the bulk of their nutrients from complete meals, with treats serving as an addition or bonus to nutritionally optimal diets.

Sources and References

  • 1 Produce Processing, August 4, 2022
  • 2 StatPearls, June 19, 2026
  • 3 USDA, January 2026
  • 4 Clin Phytosci, 6, 46 (2020)
  • 5 TasteMade, 8 Things You Didn’t Know About Oranges (Archived)
  • 6 Nutrients. 2017 Nov 3;9(11):1211
  • 7 Nutrients. 2017 Aug 12;9(8):866
  • 8 USDA FoodData Central, Oranges, raw, all commercial varieties
  • 9 Serious Facts, 40 Interesting Orange Facts (Archived)
  • 10 Rover, Can Dogs Eat Oranges?

item.title: Dogs Get This Special Care 5 Times More Often Than Cats, but Why?
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Cats in the U.S. don’t make it to the vet’s office nearly as often as their canine counterparts
  • There are many logical reasons to avoid veterinary visits, but the reality is that every cat should see a vet at least once a year
  • It’s important to find a veterinarian who doesn’t push a regular vaccine schedule or unnecessary pest control products, especially for indoor-only cats
  • It’s also important to find a kitty-friendly veterinary practice, or mobile cat practice, one that is either cats-only or follows feline-friendly handling guidelines
  • There are many things you can do as your cat’s primary advocate to improve his or her experience during veterinary visits

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published February 21, 2017.

If you share your life with a cat and a dog and are like the majority of pet parents, your canine pal sees the vet much more frequently than your cat does. In fact, according to one report, only 1 cat is seen by a veterinarian for every 5 dogs, even though there are several million more pet cats in the U.S. than dogs.1

A pet food company took a survey of over 1,000 cat and dog owners to gauge their “beliefs and motivations,” with the following results:2

  • Compared to dog owners, six times as many cat owners didn’t take their cat to the vet in 2016
  • Two-thirds of cat owners simply believe cats have fewer health issues than dogs
  • The older a cat gets, the more likely the owner is to take her to the vet only when she is sick
  • Thirty-one percent of those with a senior cat only take her to the vet when she is sick, compared to 20% for adult cats, 18% for adolescents and 17% for kittens

The lack of routine feline vet visits worries veterinarians, especially feline practitioners, and cat advocacy groups like the CATalyst Council and others. Their concern is understandable, but so are the reasons kitties don’t make it to the vet’s office all that often, including:

  • Many cats live entirely indoors, so the risk of acquiring an infectious disease or injury is extremely low
  • Cats are notoriously stoic when they don’t feel well, because they’re wired that way, so it’s difficult even for expert cat guardians to tell when kitty is sick
  • Whereas many dogs are rambunctious and accident-prone, cats are naturally cautious and much less likely to court disaster
  • The vast majority of kitties absolutely despise car rides and vet clinics, so for many cat parents, the stress of vet visits seems to outweigh any benefit their pet receives
  • Many conventional veterinarians continue to heavily promote routine re-vaccinations and pest control chemicals (flea/tick, heartworm, etc.) even for indoor-only kitties whose exposure risk is minimal. Many cat guardians don’t agree with that approach and don’t appreciate being pressured

So what’s a conscientious cat parent to do?

Recommendations for Cat Veterinary Visits

First and foremost, try to find a veterinarian whose practice philosophy you’re comfortable with. This may be a holistic or integrative veterinarian, or a conventional veterinarian who doesn’t aggressively promote vaccines, pest preventives or veterinary drugs at every visit.

Alternatively, you’ll need to advocate for your cat with your vet, and push back as necessary, politely but firmly. Keep in mind that you have the final say in what treatments and chemicals are administered to your pet.

Unfortunately, there are still many conventional practitioners who continue to over-vaccinate pets and recommend unnecessary pest control products during routine vet visits. Ideally, twice-yearly wellness visits is recommended for the following three reasons:

  1. Changes in your kitty’s health can happen in a short period of time, especially on the inside where you can’t see it, like sudden changes in kidney health
  2. Sick cats often show no signs of illness, but early detection allows for early intervention
  3. Semi-annual visits give you and your veterinarian the opportunity to closely monitor changes in your kitty’s behavior and attitude that require further investigation

At a minimum, younger healthy cats should see the vet once a year. Kitties over the age of 7 and those with chronic health conditions should be seen twice a year or more frequently if necessary.

Performing regular at-home physical exams on your cat to learn what’s normal and what’s not is also recommended. This will help you stay on top of her health, and if you can only manage an annual visit to your veterinarian, at-home exams will help alert you to changes in her health in between checkups.

Finding a Cat-Friendly Veterinary Clinic

Because veterinary visits are so stressful for cats, find either a cats-only practice or one that actively takes steps to make their feline patients as comfortable and relaxed as possible.

The American Association of Feline Practitioners (AAFP) and the International Society of Feline Medicine (ISFM) created a set of “Feline-Friendly Handling Guidelines”3 that offers suggestions for veterinarians who want to create an inviting environment for their cat patients. These include:

  • Managing clinic odors — Cats are macrosmatic, which means their very acute sense of smell drives them to behave in specific ways. Certain scents, for example, air fresheners, disinfectants and blood, can cause kitties to feel anxious or fearful.
  • Placing synthetic feline facial pheromone (FFP) analog diffusers and sprays throughout the clinic — Research shows these products have a calming effect on cats under stress, and can help reduce anxiety, fear and aggressive responses during vet visits.
  • Reducing what feline patients see and hear during visits — Keeping other people and pets out of a cat's line of sight can alleviate anxiety. If the clinic is able to provide a separate entrance and waiting room for cats, even better. Noisy environments, including loud voices, should be avoided.

    Ask the receptionist if you can wait in your car with your cat if you feel the waiting room is anything less than serene. If your cat needs to be hospitalized, ask that she be housed away from dogs and loud environments.

    Vets who treat cats and their staffs should know how to safely and effectively manage every type of kitty, from the most docile to the most “fractious” (aggressive).

    Very aggressive cats may be best managed by breathing in sevoflurane gas (similar to the “laughing gas” used for highly stressed dental patients) to reduce anxiety.

    Believe it or not, one client has an aggressive cat who comes in his own travel box (a clear Rubbermaid tub), which she equipped with two small holes that allow for oxygen and inhalant gas to be easily administered.

    This dramatically reduces stress on the cat, the cat’s owner and the entire veterinary staff because kitty’s happy coming in, happy going under and happy going home!

If you aren't comfortable with how your cat is treated or handled during vet visits, it's up to you to advocate for your kitty with the vet and staff, or find another practice more attuned to the special needs of feline patients. The least stressful way to make sure your cat is healthy without traveling at all is to consider calling a mobile vet clinic to visit your home.

Not every city or town has the luxury of a mobile veterinary service, and not every cat parent can afford the extra expense, but this is recommended for highly stressed cats when it makes sense.

5 More Tips for Better Vet Visits

  1. Do some dry runs to the veterinary clinic to help get your cat accustomed to trips in the car and the clinic environment.
  2. Get your cat used to being handled. Manipulate his paws, inspect his ears, clip his nails, open and inspect the inside of his mouth, move your hands over his legs and body and comb or brush his coat. If you do this regularly your cat will be less stressed when it’s the real thing at the vet’s office.
  3. Get your cat accustomed to a carrier. If the only time she sees the thing is for vet visits, you can’t blame her for panicking. Put her in the carrier with a few treats for five minutes a day for a week prior to the visit.

    Even consider feeding your cat in the crate, leaving the door open to encourage exploration on her own. Leave the carrier out for a week prior to the vet visit so she can inspect it. The morning of the appointment, find her well in advance of the time of your vet appointment and encourage her to enter the carrier on her own. Put an item with a familiar scent in the carrier, like her bedding or a favorite toy.
  4. Consider administering a natural calming agent like Bach Rescue Remedy or homeopathic aconitum prior to the visit. Talk with a holistic vet about specific homeopathic, herbal or nutraceutical remedies that might help address your kitty’s stress level.
  5. Keep your cool. Your kitty can sense your anxiety and stress, so remain calm. Stay positive and proceed at your cat’s pace. Tune in to how he’s responding, and use treats and other rewards to encourage desired behavior.

Sources and References

  • Royal Canin
  • 1 Banfield State of Pet Health Report, 2016 (Archived)
  • 2 Royal Canin News Release, August 18, 2016 (Archived)
  • 3 2011 AAFP/ISFM Feline-Friendly Handling Guidelines (Archived)

  • It’s important to find a veterinarian who doesn’t push a regular vaccine schedule or unnecessary pest control products, especially for indoor-only cats
  • It’s also important to find a kitty-friendly veterinary practice, or mobile cat practice, one that is either cats-only or follows feline-friendly handling guidelines
  • There are many things you can do as your cat’s primary advocate to improve his or her experience during veterinary visits

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published February 21, 2017.

If you share your life with a cat and a dog and are like the majority of pet parents, your canine pal sees the vet much more frequently than your cat does. In fact, according to one report, only 1 cat is seen by a veterinarian for every 5 dogs, even though there are several million more pet cats in the U.S. than dogs.1

A pet food company took a survey of over 1,000 cat and dog owners to gauge their “beliefs and motivations,” with the following results:2

  • Compared to dog owners, six times as many cat owners didn’t take their cat to the vet in 2016
  • Two-thirds of cat owners simply believe cats have fewer health issues than dogs
  • The older a cat gets, the more likely the owner is to take her to the vet only when she is sick
  • Thirty-one percent of those with a senior cat only take her to the vet when she is sick, compared to 20% for adult cats, 18% for adolescents and 17% for kittens

The lack of routine feline vet visits worries veterinarians, especially feline practitioners, and cat advocacy groups like the CATalyst Council and others. Their concern is understandable, but so are the reasons kitties don’t make it to the vet’s office all that often, including:

  • Many cats live entirely indoors, so the risk of acquiring an infectious disease or injury is extremely low
  • Cats are notoriously stoic when they don’t feel well, because they’re wired that way, so it’s difficult even for expert cat guardians to tell when kitty is sick
  • Whereas many dogs are rambunctious and accident-prone, cats are naturally cautious and much less likely to court disaster
  • The vast majority of kitties absolutely despise car rides and vet clinics, so for many cat parents, the stress of vet visits seems to outweigh any benefit their pet receives
  • Many conventional veterinarians continue to heavily promote routine re-vaccinations and pest control chemicals (flea/tick, heartworm, etc.) even for indoor-only kitties whose exposure risk is minimal. Many cat guardians don’t agree with that approach and don’t appreciate being pressured

So what’s a conscientious cat parent to do?

Recommendations for Cat Veterinary Visits

First and foremost, try to find a veterinarian whose practice philosophy you’re comfortable with. This may be a holistic or integrative veterinarian, or a conventional veterinarian who doesn’t aggressively promote vaccines, pest preventives or veterinary drugs at every visit.

Alternatively, you’ll need to advocate for your cat with your vet, and push back as necessary, politely but firmly. Keep in mind that you have the final say in what treatments and chemicals are administered to your pet.

Unfortunately, there are still many conventional practitioners who continue to over-vaccinate pets and recommend unnecessary pest control products during routine vet visits. Ideally, twice-yearly wellness visits is recommended for the following three reasons:

  1. Changes in your kitty’s health can happen in a short period of time, especially on the inside where you can’t see it, like sudden changes in kidney health
  2. Sick cats often show no signs of illness, but early detection allows for early intervention
  3. Semi-annual visits give you and your veterinarian the opportunity to closely monitor changes in your kitty’s behavior and attitude that require further investigation

Performing regular at-home physical exams on your cat to learn what’s normal and what’s not is also recommended. This will help you stay on top of her health, and if you can only manage an annual visit to your veterinarian, at-home exams will help alert you to changes in her health in between checkups.

Finding a Cat-Friendly Veterinary Clinic

Because veterinary visits are so stressful for cats, find either a cats-only practice or one that actively takes steps to make their feline patients as comfortable and relaxed as possible.

The American Association of Feline Practitioners (AAFP) and the International Society of Feline Medicine (ISFM) created a set of “Feline-Friendly Handling Guidelines”3 that offers suggestions for veterinarians who want to create an inviting environment for their cat patients. These include:

  • Placing synthetic feline facial pheromone (FFP) analog diffusers and sprays throughout the clinic — Research shows these products have a calming effect on cats under stress, and can help reduce anxiety, fear and aggressive responses during vet visits.
  • Reducing what feline patients see and hear during visits — Keeping other people and pets out of a cat's line of sight can alleviate anxiety. If the clinic is able to provide a separate entrance and waiting room for cats, even better. Noisy environments, including loud voices, should be avoided.

    Ask the receptionist if you can wait in your car with your cat if you feel the waiting room is anything less than serene. If your cat needs to be hospitalized, ask that she be housed away from dogs and loud environments.

    Vets who treat cats and their staffs should know how to safely and effectively manage every type of kitty, from the most docile to the most “fractious” (aggressive).

    Very aggressive cats may be best managed by breathing in sevoflurane gas (similar to the “laughing gas” used for highly stressed dental patients) to reduce anxiety.

    Believe it or not, one client has an aggressive cat who comes in his own travel box (a clear Rubbermaid tub), which she equipped with two small holes that allow for oxygen and inhalant gas to be easily administered.

    This dramatically reduces stress on the cat, the cat’s owner and the entire veterinary staff because kitty’s happy coming in, happy going under and happy going home!

If you aren't comfortable with how your cat is treated or handled during vet visits, it's up to you to advocate for your kitty with the vet and staff, or find another practice more attuned to the special needs of feline patients. The least stressful way to make sure your cat is healthy without traveling at all is to consider calling a mobile vet clinic to visit your home.

Not every city or town has the luxury of a mobile veterinary service, and not every cat parent can afford the extra expense, but this is recommended for highly stressed cats when it makes sense.

5 More Tips for Better Vet Visits

  1. Do some dry runs to the veterinary clinic to help get your cat accustomed to trips in the car and the clinic environment.
  2. Get your cat used to being handled. Manipulate his paws, inspect his ears, clip his nails, open and inspect the inside of his mouth, move your hands over his legs and body and comb or brush his coat. If you do this regularly your cat will be less stressed when it’s the real thing at the vet’s office.
  3. Get your cat accustomed to a carrier. If the only time she sees the thing is for vet visits, you can’t blame her for panicking. Put her in the carrier with a few treats for five minutes a day for a week prior to the visit.

    Even consider feeding your cat in the crate, leaving the door open to encourage exploration on her own. Leave the carrier out for a week prior to the vet visit so she can inspect it. The morning of the appointment, find her well in advance of the time of your vet appointment and encourage her to enter the carrier on her own. Put an item with a familiar scent in the carrier, like her bedding or a favorite toy.
  4. Consider administering a natural calming agent like Bach Rescue Remedy or homeopathic aconitum prior to the visit. Talk with a holistic vet about specific homeopathic, herbal or nutraceutical remedies that might help address your kitty’s stress level.
  5. Keep your cool. Your kitty can sense your anxiety and stress, so remain calm. Stay positive and proceed at your cat’s pace. Tune in to how he’s responding, and use treats and other rewards to encourage desired behavior.

  • 2 Royal Canin News Release, August 18, 2016 (Archived)
  • 3 2011 AAFP/ISFM Feline-Friendly Handling Guidelines (Archived)

item.title: Why Vets Reach for This Vitamin in an Emergency
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Vitamin K1 (phytonadione) is the targeted antidote veterinarians reach for when a dog has been exposed to anticoagulant rat or mouse poisons. It restores the body's ability to activate the clotting proteins disrupted by the poison
  • Anticoagulant rodenticides are dangerously deceptive: A dog can look completely normal for three to seven days after exposure before serious internal bleeding shows up, which is why waiting for symptoms is one of the riskiest things you can do
  • Not all "vitamin K" is the same. K1 is the natural, plant-derived form used therapeutically; K2 is produced by gut bacteria and is linked to bone biology; and K3 is a synthetic compound used in feeds and is not interchangeable with the others
  • Treatment typically involves about 30 days of vitamin K1 therapy plus clotting tests, because "superwarfarin" rodenticides linger in the body for weeks, stopping early, even when the dog looks great, can let bleeding restart
  • Vitamin K is not a general-purpose blood booster; it won't treat anemia, low platelet counts, or inherited clotting disorders, and the over-the-counter version isn't equivalent to the prescription K1 that vets use; suspected rodenticide exposure is always an emergency-room conversation, not a home-treatment one

You discover a chewed-up box of rat poison behind the shed. Your dog seems fine, wagging, hungry, totally normal. So you take a breath and tell yourself it is probably okay. Then you call your vet and learn something you did not expect: This is exactly the kind of situation where every hour matters, and the treatment you might need is not a heavy-duty drug at all, but a vitamin.

Vitamin K, specifically vitamin K1, is one of the most important tools veterinarians have when a dog has been exposed to certain rat and mouse poisons. It is a quiet hero of the emergency-medicine world: low-drama, well-tolerated, and able to reverse a poisoning that would otherwise be fatal. Here is what is worth knowing about it.

What Vitamin K Actually Does

Vitamin K is a fat-soluble vitamin best known for one critical job: helping the body make proteins needed for normal blood clotting. Clotting is the process that stops bleeding after an injury. It depends on a chain of proteins produced by the liver, and several of those proteins simply cannot work until vitamin K activates them. Without active vitamin K in the system, the body may still make clotting proteins, but they are functionally useless.1

Vitamin K also plays a role in proteins involved in bone biology and calcium regulation, which is why you sometimes see it mentioned in conversations about skeletal health. But the reason it shows up in emergencies is the clotting side of the equation.

To work properly, vitamin K needs healthy fat digestion. It is absorbed alongside dietary fat through the same pathways that handle vitamins A, D, and E. That means anything that disrupts fat absorption, such as chronic gut disease, certain liver conditions, or problems with bile flow, can interfere with vitamin K status even when the diet itself looks fine.2,3

The 3 Forms and Their Different Roles

Vitamin K is actually a family of related compounds, and the form matters a lot in veterinary medicine. Here are the different classifications of vitamin K.4

  • Vitamin K1 (phytonadione) is the natural form found in green plants. This is the form veterinarians use therapeutically.
  • Vitamin K2 (menaquinone) is produced by gut bacteria and found in some fermented or animal foods. It’s often discussed in bone and calcium nutrition.
  • Vitamin K3 (menadione) is a synthetic vitamin K-active compound used in some animal feeds. It’s not interchangeable with K1 or K2.

When a vet talks about giving vitamin K after a poisoning, they almost always mean vitamin K1. It is the form that effectively restores the body's ability to activate the clotting proteins that the poison has knocked offline.5,6

Why Rat Poison Is Such a Sneaky Threat

Many rat and mouse poisons are designed as anticoagulant rodenticides. They kill rodents by interfering with vitamin K recycling, the body's natural system for reusing vitamin K to keep activating clotting proteins over time.

When that recycling system goes down, clotting proteins gradually lose function. Existing active proteins get used up, and no new functional ones replace them. After several days, the bleeding can become catastrophic, sometimes external, sometimes internal, and often hard to spot until things are very wrong.7

The poisons most commonly used today are sometimes called superwarfarins. They behave like prescription blood-thinner medications, but at much higher potency, and they can keep thinning the blood for three to five days or longer. That is why these poisonings are so dangerous: the effect builds quietly, and once severe bleeding starts, the window for intervention is small.8,9

The Delayed-Symptom Problem

Here is the part that catches a lot of pet parents off guard: A dog that has eaten anticoagulant rat poison usually looks completely normal in the first day or two. They may even seem fine for nearly a week.10

This is because outward signs of poisoning often do not appear until three to seven days after ingestion. By then, internal bleeding may be well underway. Possible signs include:11,12

  • Lethargy or sudden weakness
  • Pale gums
  • Difficulty breathing or coughing
  • Bloody stools or urine
  • Unexplained bruising or swelling under the skin
  • Nosebleeds
  • Prolonged bleeding from minor wounds
  • Vomiting, sometimes with blood
  • Collapse

Because symptoms are delayed, the rule with rodenticide exposure is simple: Do not wait. Even if your dog seems fine, call your veterinarian or animal poison control as soon as you suspect exposure. The earlier treatment starts, the better the outcome.

Why Vitamin K1 Is the Antidote

Vitamin K1 works by going around the poison's blocked recycling pathway and supplying the body with a fresh source of usable vitamin K. With enough K1 on board, the liver can resume making functional clotting proteins, and the bleeding risk is brought back under control.13

It is a beautifully targeted treatment. The poison removes the body's ability to activate clotting proteins. The antidote replaces what the poison disabled. There are not many antidotes in veterinary medicine that work this cleanly.

Reports of vitamin K1 overdose in dogs are very uncommon, especially when it is used under veterinary supervision. Its synthetic cousin, vitamin K3, has a less favorable safety profile and is not used for this purpose. That is part of why the form matters so much, and why over-the-counter vitamin K supplements are not an equivalent product.14

What Treatment Looks Like

Treatment depends on how recently the dog ate the poison, how much was eaten, and which active ingredient was involved. A typical approach can include:

  • Decontamination — If exposure was recent (usually within a couple of hours), your vet may induce vomiting and give activated charcoal to limit absorption.
  • Vitamin K1 therapy — This is the heart of the treatment. K1 may be given by injection initially, especially if the dog is already symptomatic, and then continued as oral tablets or capsules at home.

    Because superwarfarins linger in the body for weeks, vitamin K1 is typically given for about 30 days. Stopping early, even when the dog looks great, can cause bleeding to restart.
  • Bloodwork and clotting tests — Your vet will likely check clotting times during and after treatment to confirm the therapy is working, and the body has cleared the poison.
  • Supportive care — Dogs who are already bleeding may need IV fluids, plasma, or even a blood transfusion to stabilize them while the vitamin K does its job.

Remember: Do Not DIY This

The form of vitamin K1 used to treat anticoagulant rodenticide poisoning is not sold over the counter. It requires a veterinary prescription, and the dose, route, and length of treatment all depend on the type of poison and the dog's clotting status.

Casual vitamin K from a supplement aisle is not the same product, is not dosed for this purpose, and may not contain the right form. Worse, it can give pet parents false confidence and delay the urgent veterinary care that actually saves lives.

And not all rat poisons work the same way. Some affect the nervous system or calcium balance instead of clotting, and vitamin K1 will not help with those. That is another reason the product label, the exposure timing, and a vet's evaluation all matter.15

What to Do if You Suspect Exposure

If you find evidence that your dog has eaten rat or mouse bait, or even if you just suspect it. Follow these reminders:

  • Collect any packaging or bait you can find. The active ingredient on the label tells the vet exactly what they are dealing with.
  • Note when the exposure may have happened and roughly how much your dog may have eaten.
  • Call your vet, the nearest emergency hospital, or an animal poison hotline immediately; do not wait for symptoms to appear.
  • Do not try to induce vomiting at home unless specifically instructed to do so by a professional.
  • Bring your dog in for evaluation, even if they look completely fine.

Pet Poison Helpline (855-764-7661) and the ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center are good resources to keep saved in your phone.

Vitamin K Outside the Emergency Room

Vitamin K1 emergencies are the most dramatic story, but vitamin K also matters in everyday biology. Healthy dogs eating complete, balanced diets generally get enough vitamin K from their food and from compounds produced by gut bacteria. Routine vitamin K supplementation is not supported by strong evidence in healthy dogs. However, it does deserve a closer look in dogs with:16

  • Poor fat digestion or malabsorption
  • Liver disease or bile flow problems
  • Long-term gastrointestinal disease
  • Prolonged antibiotic use that disrupts gut bacteria
  • Homemade or incomplete diets
  • Unexplained bruising or abnormal clotting tests

Because vitamin K is fat-soluble, it depends on healthy fat digestion and bile flow for absorption. Dogs with chronic digestive or liver issues may run lower than expected, even if their diet looks fine on paper.

One more thing worth knowing: Vitamin K is not a general-purpose blood booster. It will not raise red blood cell counts or treat anemia from other causes. It also will not help with bleeding caused by low platelets, autoimmune conditions, or inherited clotting disorders. The strongest evidence for vitamin K use in dogs sits squarely in the rodenticide-exposure setting.17

The Bottom Line

When veterinarians reach for vitamin K in an emergency, they are not handing out a supplement. They are using a precisely targeted antidote to one of the most common and most deceptive poisonings in companion animals. Anticoagulant rat poisons are designed to hide their damage for days. Vitamin K1, given early enough and continued long enough, is what flips that script.

If you suspect your dog has been exposed to rat or mouse bait, do not wait for symptoms and do not try to manage it at home. Call your vet or a pet poison hotline, bring the packaging if you can, and let the professionals do what this particular vitamin does best: buy your dog back the time their clotting system needs to recover.

Sources and References

  • 2,4,7,12,15,16 Bernie’s University, June 9, 2026
  • 3,5,8,10,11,13,14 Pet Poison Hotline, Vitamin K1 for Dogs

item.title: This Beautiful Pet Will Favor Your Lap Over Most Anything Else
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Himalayan cats are a hybrid breed developed by crossing the Persian and Siamese breeds
  • “Himmys” as they are often called, are built more like Persians than Siamese and have the Persian temperament of preferring naps to exercise
  • If you’re thinking of adding a Himalayan to your family, be sure to check your local shelters and rescue organizations first to see if there’s an adoptable cat available
  • Himalayans are prone to health issues tied to their flat facial structure, including breathing difficulties, dental malocclusions, eye conditions and polycystic kidney disease
  • Daily grooming is important for Himalayans; their coat needs combing every day and a bath at least once a month

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published September 4, 2015.

Himalayan cats are a hybrid breed developed by crossing the Persian and Siamese breeds.

“Himmys” as they are often called, are built more like Persians than Siamese and have the Persian temperament of preferring naps to exercise. If you’re thinking of adding a Himalayan to your family, be sure to check your local shelters and rescue organizations first to see if there’s an adoptable cat available.

8 Cool Facts About Himalayan Cats

  1. Himalayans are hybrids


    The beautiful and unusual-looking Himalayan is a blend of the Persian and Siamese breeds and was developed through human intervention. Some cat fanciers think of the Himalayan as a distinct breed; others consider it a variety of the Persian breed.

    Himalayans have the characteristic flat, open faces of Persians. The eyes are a beautiful bright blue, and the ears are small and perky. There is a distinctive ruff around the neck that looks similar to a lion’s mane. Their bodies right down to their paws are large and fluffy.

    The Himalayan is often referred to as the “Himmy,” and has been called “a Persian in Siamese drag.”1

item.title: The World's Smallest Dog Has a Big Secret
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • The Chihuahua is the smallest dog breed in the world. Unfortunately, some breeders are creating Chihuahuas so tiny their health is severely compromised
  • Chis tend to be one-person dogs who are fiercely loyal to their human
  • Chihuahuas are one of the longest-lived breeds, despite their genetic predisposition to several health problems
  • Chis are active, fun-loving little dogs that need daily exercise and close supervision both indoors and outside
  • If you’re thinking of adding a Chihuahua to your family, be sure to check your local shelters and rescue organizations for adoptable dogs

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published October 16, 2015.

The Chihuahua is the smallest dog breed in the world. Unfortunately, some breeders are creating Chihuahuas so tiny their health is severely compromised. Chis tend to be one-person dogs who are fiercely loyal to their human.

Chihuahuas are one of the longest-lived breeds, despite their genetic predisposition to several health problems. Chis are active, fun-loving little dogs that need daily exercise and close supervision both indoors and outside.

If you're thinking of adding a Chihuahua to your family, be sure to check your local shelters and rescue organizations for adoptable dogs.

  1. The Chihuahua is the smallest dog breed in the world


    Even well-bred, healthy Chihuahuas are quite small, with average-size adults weighing just 4 to 6 pounds and standing a mere 6 to 10 inches high.

    Unfortunately, many disreputable people interested primarily in making money off their dogs deliberately breed Chis that will only weigh 1 to 2 pounds as adults. These dogs are advertised as "miniature" or "teacup," and while they may look adorable, they are typically very frail. Their bones are exceedingly thin and prone to sprains and breaks.

    Too-small Chihuahuas are also at greater risk for tracheal collapse, food intolerances, failure to thrive, and several other disorders.
  2. Chihuahuas also have one of the longest lifespans of all dog breeds


    Not only are Chis the smallest of all dog breeds, but they also outlive most of them. The average lifespan of a Chihuahua is 12 to 20 years, in part because of his small size (giant breed dogs have the shortest lifespans), and also thanks to his relatively good health compared to other breeds.
  3. Chihuahuas are named after Chihuahua, Mexico


    Chihuahua is the largest northern state in Mexico, where the breed is called the chihuahueño.

    In the late 1800s, U.S. travelers to Mexico discovered the breed and brought some of the dogs back to the states. Before they became known as Chihuahuas, members of the breed that were discovered along the U.S. border with Mexico were called Arizona or Texas dogs.
  4. The Chihuahua's history is a bit of a mystery


    The most common theory about the origins of the breed is that Chihuahuas are descendants of the Techichi, a companion dog kept by the Toltec civilization in Mexico.

    It is speculated that earlier ancestors of the breed were present prior to the Mayans, because depictions of dogs very similar to the Chihuahua have been unearthed at the Great Pyramid of Cholula that predates 1530, and at the ruins of Chichen Itza on the Yucatan Peninsula as well.

    The Chihuahua has been consistently popular in the U.S. since its arrival and was first recognized by the American Kennel Club in 1904.
  5. Chihuahuas can be either smooth- or long-coated


    Rumor has it that long-coated Chis may have been created by crossing Chihuahuas with Yorkshire Terriers. Unlike many long-haired breeds, long-coated Chis require minimal grooming. In addition, dogs with a long coat typically shed less than smooth-coated Chihuahuas. It can take 3+ years before a full long-haired coat develops.

    The AKC lists over 40 different coat colors and markings in Chihuahuas, including black, black-and-tan, white, cream, chocolate, and red. In fact, Chis come in a wider variety of coat colors than any other breed.
  6. Chihuahuas are one-person dogs and prefer other Chis as friends


    As with most dogs, a Chihuahua owner's temperament greatly influences his or her pet's temperament. Chis tend to be one-person dogs who develop a fierce loyalty to one family member. This can lead to over-protectiveness, especially when other people and pets are around. For this reason, Chihuahuas aren't considered a good choice for homes with small children.

    Chis are reported to be "clannish," preferring the company of Chihuahuas or Chihuahua mixes to other dog breeds.
  7. Chihuahuas are not cold-weather dogs


    Chihuahuas tend to shiver or tremble when stressed, excited, or cold. The smooth-coated variety, in particular, doesn't tolerate cold well and may need a sweater during the cooler months of the year.

    Expect to find your little heat-seeking guy or girl napping in a sunny spot, under a blanket, curled up in a tight ball, or on your lap. Chihuahuas are also true den dwellers and will often burrow into pillows, clothes hampers, and blankets. This is an ideal dog to crate-train, as she will view her own private "den" as a place of warmth, comfort, and safety.
  8. Many Chihuahuas have a soft spot in their skulls


    These soft spots are called moleras (an open fontanelle), and Chis are the only breed born with an incomplete skull. It isn't a birth defect, but rather a normal adaptation that helps the puppy pass through the birth canal.

    Chihuahuas with rounder heads more often have moleras, but the soft spots are present in almost all Chi puppies. The molera normally closes by the time a puppy is 6 months old, but some never close completely. Occasionally, a molera is mistaken for hydrocephalus ("water on the brain").
  9. Chihuahuas are predisposed to certain health problems


    All dog breeds are prone to certain disorders and diseases, and Chihuahuas are no exception. Commonly seen conditions in Chis include hypoglycemia (low blood sugar), eye problems, collapsed trachea, dental issues, luxating patella (floating kneecap), and heart-related disorders.
  10. Chihuahuas may be small in size, but they have big personalities


    A Chi's first love is to be close to his person. These little dogs also tend to be busy and fun loving, and will happily (though often nervously) accompany their owners wherever they go. They need at least 20 to 30 minutes of exercise each day.

    Chihuahuas are affectionate, smart, and fast learners. You'll find them competing in agility and obedience events just like the big dogs. As with any dog, positive reinforcement behavior training is the way to get the best out of your little Chi.
  11. Chihuahuas are much easier to lose than other breeds


    It's important to always remember that your Chi is a very small dog who is naturally curious and may go on solo "adventures" given the chance. Chihuahuas have escaped from even the most secure yards and enclosures through impossibly small gaps in or under fencing.

    Chihuahuas are also frequently stepped on or played with too roughly, causing injury, so everyone in the household need to remain vigilant. These dogs often don't realize how small they are, and will take on even very large, aggressive dogs. It's also important to protect your Chi from potential predators like coyotes and birds of prey.
  12. Animal shelters in some areas of the U.S. are loaded with Chihuahuas


    Sadly, Chihuahuas seem to be a popular choice of people who aren't committed to sterilizing their dogs and/or who breed them for profit. Consequently, in some areas of the U.S., particularly the western states, shelters are filled with homeless Chihuahuas.

    If you're thinking of adding a Chi to your family, check your local shelters and rescue organizations first, as well as Petfinder. There are hundreds and perhaps even thousands of these little dogs looking for homes, and when you adopt a homeless Chihuahua, you help put backyard and puppy mill breeders out of business.

Sources and References

  • Mom.me
  • Wikipedia, Chihuahua (dog breed)
  • Dogtime.com, Chihuahua
